prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 position: a sole prize for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B014) to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. I moved from my own opening first choice, IceCube, to this after the openings, and the full round-1 exchange has not given me a reason to move back or to add a second part. What persuades me is that nature supplied a clue to a concrete idea. The 2011 continuum model said where to look, a single twist angle at which the Dirac velocity vanishes, and in 2018 correlated insulators and superconductivity appeared there, in a system tuned by a gate voltage and an angle. Many groups have since reproduced the phases with transport, STM and compressibility probes and carried the idea into other moire systems. The citation I would defend names the predicted flat bands and the observed phases, and says nothing about the pairing mechanism. Five members already name the same three people, so the committee is arguing about two specific attribution questions and not about the science.
statement.case_against: Two reservations remain and I will not hide them. First, the superconductivity is not understood and the field is under a decade old. I have said that big ideas can take a long time to prove their worth, so I take Lindroth and Kroll seriously. My answer is that a claim about the discovery of the phases does not depend on the mechanism, but a prize this young leaves little room for the interpretation to turn out different from what we assume. Second, attribution: Eva Andrei's STM and transport work on flat-band localisation and Yuan Cao's first authorship of the 2018 papers fall outside any three-person cut, and no one in this committee has resolved the Andrei question. I now treat the expert report on it as a condition of my vote. If it shows that her results established the flat-band physics independently of and before the 2018 transport work, I would have to consider Andrei in place of Bistritzer, and I would then want the committee to look again at whether the prediction half of the citation can stand.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps the optical lattice clock (B013, Katori and Ye) first, and the chair asks whether she and Kroll regard the open pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder in B014 as a maturity bar and what would move them.
responses.response: I share your caution but I draw the line elsewhere. The maturity test I would apply is whether the phenomenon is robust, not whether it is explained, and the correlated and superconducting phases have been seen by many groups. The 2018 result is also more than a prediction confirmed: the flat-band model does not itself predict the insulators or the superconductor, so the experiment is the original step. On the clock, you and Kroll both answer the discovery-versus-capability question by pointing to redshift tests, varying-constant limits and dark-matter searches. Those are the future payoffs I would want to see delivered before I call it a discovery, so my view of B013 is unchanged. I would not block it if the expert reports show the first lattice-clock demonstrations clearly separate Katori and Ye from the frequency-comb lineage.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, proposes a two-part prize of IceCube (Halzen alone) with lattice clocks, concedes that B016 has the thinnest support, and says the part should not carry the prize unless experts supply a defensible set of names.
responses.response: I opened with B016 first and I still think neutrino astronomy is the kind of new observational window the prize exists for. But I agree with your own caveat and take it further: a single name for a km3 detector with AMANDA behind it is not something I would defend in public on this packet. I disagree with you on the source question, which matters more to me than it does to you. The diffuse flux is a detection, but the first identified source (TXS 0506+056) and the Galactic plane are what turned it into astronomy. A B016 part would also need a citation written around the flux and the sources, and I do not see a two-part prize being justified only to give IceCube a partner. If the experts return a defensible credit set, I would vote for B016 as a second part, and until then it stays my first alternative. I would also say you should let the committee rule on your possible recusal and not decide it alone.

responses.point: Johansson asks whether the committee could responsibly build a configuration on the single credited name for B016 without outside expert input, and whether B016 could pair with another part. He also declares a connection to B046 and says he should recuse from any vote on it.
responses.response: No, not on a single name from the packet alone, and I do not think the committee should. Building a prize on Halzen alone would credit a collaboration-scale discovery on the packet's say-so, which is the kind of choice the expert reports exist to check. Pairing does not fix that, because a second part cannot supply the missing credit for the first. On B046, I accept your recusal and I agree the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes the case hard. I would only add that your moving to B014 on the strength of the discovery is a good sign for the committee's reasoning.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B014 but raises priority and fairness toward earlier twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell, Shallcross), and notes the continuum model is a minimal effective description that a prize might over-credit.
responses.response: This is a point I had not weighed enough. Your concern about earlier twisted-bilayer theory is real, and I would write the citation to guard against it: the prediction credited is the flat bands at magic angles in the continuum model, and the citation should not claim the later understanding of the correlations. That fits what I think the prize is for, namely a clue from nature confirming a concrete prediction. I also agree with you that Bistritzer should stay, and with Olsson that making room for Andrei by dropping a theorist would weaken the prediction-then-experiment structure. I would only do that if the expert report on the Andrei question forces it.

responses.point: Olsson supports B014 but wants an expert report on priority between Andrei's group and the 2018 transport work before a final decision, and says she must be absolutely sure who did the original work.
responses.response: I agree and would put the same two questions to the experts: did Andrei's STM evidence of flat-band localisation establish the flat-band physics before and independently of the 2018 transport results, and does Cao's role as first author alter the choice at the experimental end of the cut? I would add a third, from Eriksson's round-1 reading: if the answer to the first is a partial yes, can the citation be worded so that it credits the correlated phases and not the flat-band evidence, which would leave the trio intact? I would rather hold the vote on that report than guess from our memories of dates, which the chair reminds us are unreliable.

uncertainties: Whether Eva Andrei's STM and transport work on flat-band localisation was independent of and prior to the 2018 transport results, and whether Yuan Cao's first authorship changes the experimental credit.
Whether the open pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder make a prize for a field under a decade old premature, even though the phases are robust.
Whether earlier twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell, Shallcross) weakens the priority of the 2011 continuum model.
Whether outside experts can supply a defensible multi-person credit set for B016, and I recall AMANDA-era and collaboration roles from memory only.
Whether B041 is too close to the 2016 topological prize and leaves out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Mele and Fu.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I find no specific conflict from my profile with any shortlisted candidate or credited name: my work is in string theory, cosmology and black holes, and my connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala group) have no stated link to the shortlist. I note Johansson's declared recusal from B046 and Pearce's possible recusal question on B016, both for the committee to rule on.
